case.case_title: Thilayanadan and Others v. Capt. Thilakaratne and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application Nos. 970/97 and 971/97, decided on 11 November 1998

clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the detention of the petitioners without a legal order violated Article 13(2) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners claimed their detention was unlawful and violated Article 13(2) as they were held without proper legal authority.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioners were produced before a Magistrate promptly and the detention was lawful under Emergency Regulations.
key_facts: Petitioners were arrested by Army personnel and handed over to police.
Petitioners were produced before the Magistrate of Mannar on 1 November 1997 and remanded.
Detention was pursuant to Emergency Regulations and related to suspicion of illegal transport of goods.
The Court examined whether the detention complied with constitutional safeguards.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court interpreted Article 13(2) as requiring that any detained person be brought before a judicial authority without undue delay and that detention must be authorized by law.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the petitioners were produced before the Magistrate promptly after arrest and that the detention was authorized under Emergency Regulations, thus complying with Article 13(2).
principles_established: Detention must be followed by prompt production before a judicial officer.
Legal authority such as Emergency Regulations can justify detention.
Constitutional safeguards require judicial oversight of detention.

outcome.holding: The Court held there was no violation of Article 13(2) and dismissed the petitioners' claim.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) was central to determining whether the petitioners' detention was lawful and constitutionally valid, impacting the Court's dismissal of the fundamental rights claim.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioners were produced before the Magistrate on 1 November 1997 and remanded, satisfying the requirements of Article 13(2).
